Reincarnation: Concept of rebirth in different physical form.

Born in Paris to a family of Georgian political refugees, this career diplomat became the first woman ever elected president of her adopted country — who is she?

Touched off by the staged 1931 Mukden incident and the puppet state of Manchukuo, this 1937–1945 conflict — China's largest war of the 20th century — is often called the start of World War II in Asia. What was it?
Second Sino-Japanese War: 1937–1945 conflict in East Asia. It is often regarded as the beginning of World War II in Asia, as the wars became heavily intertwined after Japan's entry into World War II.

Known as 'The Destroyer' within the Hindu trinity alongside Brahma and Vishnu, this deity is the Supreme Lord who creates, protects, and transforms the universe in one major tradition. Who is this god?
Shiva: Major deity in Hinduism. Shiva is one of the five equivalent deities in Panchayatana puja of the Smarta tradition of Hinduism.
A Thracian gladiator born near the Strymon river, this figure led an escaped-slave uprising against the Roman Republic known as the Third Servile War — who was he?
Spartacus: Thracian gladiator who led a slave revolt. Spartacus is described to be born near the Strymon river, in Thrace (now known as Bulgaria), possibly from the Maedi tribe.
Sparked by Arab Spring protests against Bashar al-Assad in March 2011, this nearly 14-year conflict ended with the regime's fall in December 2024 — what is it?
Syrian civil war: 2011–2024 armed conflict in Syria.

Ruling the Ostrogothic Kingdom of Italy from 493 to 526 and later regent of the Visigoths too, this king received the old Western imperial regalia from Constantinople and was addressed by Italy's aristocracy as princeps. Who was he?
Theodoric the Great: King of Italy from 493 to 526. As ruler of the combined Gothic realms, Theodoric controlled an empire stretching from the Atlantic Ocean to the Adriatic Sea.

Breaking out in 1990 between Moldovan government forces and pro-separatist fighters backed by Russia's 14th Army, this conflict over a breakaway region ended with a ceasefire in July 1992 that still holds — which conflict?
Transnistrian War: 1990–1992 separatist conflict in Moldova. Cojocaru, the Moldovan defeat in this war directly led to implementation of Moldovan neutrality.

Sparked by a suppressed student demonstration in Prague on International Students' Day in November 1989, this peaceful transfer of power ended 41 years of one-party rule in Czechoslovakia — what was it called?
Velvet Revolution: Democratization process in Czechoslovakia in 1989.
This Chinese diplomat served as ambassador to Japan before becoming Minister of Foreign Affairs and later director of the Communist Party's Central Foreign Affairs Commission Office — who is he?
Raised in Liverpool as the half-nephew of a Nazi dictator, this man later fought against his own uncle's regime in the US Navy — who is he, after changing his name postwar?
William Stuart-Houston: Half-nephew of Adolf Hitler (1911–1987)
A Hindu monk who became Uttar Pradesh's longest-serving and first two-term chief minister, he won five straight terms from Gorakhpur after entering parliament at just 26 — who is he?
Yogi Adityanath: Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh since 2017.
Who wrote Universal Declaration of Human Rights?

Universal Declaration of Human Rights → United Nations General Assembly. All 193 member states of the UN have ratified at least one of the nine binding treaties influenced by the Declaration, with the vast majority ratifying four or more.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Who among these was born first?
Saint Valentine (born 175) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Jabir ibn Hayyan (born 721) is the earliest of the four. The c. 215 treatises that survive today mainly deal with alchemy and chemistry, magic, and Shi'ite religious philosophy.
Which of these four has been around longest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language;) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
Which of these four appeared earliest?
MUMPS (published 1966) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the physicist from these four.
Paul Ehrenfest is a physicist. Suffering from depression, in 1933 Ehrenfest killed his disabled son, Wassik, and then himself.
Which of these is a chemist?
Karen Silkwood is a chemist. The company settled out of court for US$1.38 million, while not admitting liability.
What is the atomic number of Magnesium?
Magnesium is a chemical element; it has symbol Mg and atomic number 12.
In what year was Jean Tatlock born?
Jean Tatlock: Jean Frances Tatlock (February 21, 1914 – January 4, 1944) was an American psychiatrist.
In what year was Guglielmo Marconi born?
Guglielmo Marconi: In 1929, he was ennobled as a marquess (Italian: marchese) by King Victor Emmanuel III, thus becoming the 1st Marchese di Marconi.
In what year was Sam Altman born?
Sam Altman: Altman attended Stanford University for two years before he dropped out and co-founded Loopt, a smartphone geosocial networking service.
In what year did Ernest Lawrence die?
Ernest Lawrence: A graduate of the University of South Dakota and University of Minnesota, Lawrence obtained a PhD in physics at Yale in 1925.
In what year did Johann Wolfgang von Goethe die?
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (28 August 1749 – 22 March 1832) was a German polymath who is widely regarded as the most influential writer in the German language.
In what year was Coriolis force discovered?
Coriolis force: In physics, the Coriolis force is a pseudo-force that acts on objects in motion within a frame of reference that rotates with respect to an inertial frame.
TeX: Donald Knuth. TeX is a popular means of typesetting complex mathematical formulae; it has been noted as one of the most sophisticated digital typographical systems.
Methotrexate: Pfizer. Methotrexate, formerly known as amethopterin, is a chemotherapy agent and immune-system suppressant.
Which country is Bombardier Global Express from?
Bombardier Global Express: Canada. The Bombardier Global Express is a large cabin, long-range business jet designed and manufactured by Bombardier Aviation.
Who is credited with discovering Infrared?
Infrared: William Herschel. Infrared (IR; sometimes called infrared light) is electromagnetic radiation (EMR) with wavelengths longer than that of visible light but shorter than microwaves.
Who is credited with discovering Cherenkov radiation?
Cherenkov radiation: Sergey Vavilov. A classic example of Cherenkov radiation is the characteristic blue glow of an underwater nuclear reactor.
Who is credited with discovering Argon?
Argon: William Ramsay. Argon is a chemical element; it has symbol Ar and atomic number 18.

A central nervous system stimulant of the phenethylamine class, this combo medication is approved for narcolepsy and ADHD — but is also taken as an appetite suppressant and cognitive enhancer. What is it?
Adderall is the brand name of a fixed-dose combination medication used for the treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and narcolepsy.
These organic compounds, formed when one or more hydrogens in ammonia are replaced by carbon-based groups, are defined by their carbon-nitrogen bonds — what's this class of compounds called?
Amine (UK also) are organic compounds that contain carbon-nitrogen bonds.
NATO codenamed 'Curl' and nicknamed 'Nastia' in the USSR, this twin-engine turboprop transport was later license-built in China as the Xi'an Y-7 — what is it?

Antonov An-26 (NATO reporting name: Curl, nicknamed Nastia in the USSR) is a twin-engined turboprop regional airliner and military transport aircraft, designed and produced in the Soviet Union from 1969 to 1986.
Which genus of early hominins, which lived in Africa during the Pliocene and Early Pleistocene, gave rise to the genera Homo, Paranthropus, and Kenyanthropus?
Australopithecus (-loh-; or, os-, from Latin australis southern 'grc' and (pthkos) ape) is a genus of early hominins that existed in Africa during the Pliocene and Early Pleistocene.
Often called a 'chest cold,' this inflammation of the airways in the lungs typically follows an infection that spreads down from the nose or throat. What condition is it?
Biceps is a large muscle that lies on the front of the upper arm between the shoulder and the elbow.
Located in the head in most animals with nervous systems, this organ receives sensory information, generates thought and cognition, and coordinates the body's muscles and glands — name the organ?
Brain is an organ that serves as the center of the nervous system in all vertebrate and most invertebrate animals.
Caused by an overgrowth of a common yeast, this fungal infection is known as thrush when it affects the mouth and can also cause a genital yeast infection — name the condition?
Candidiasis is a fungal infection due to any species of yeasts in the genus Candida or those that were formerly classified in genus Candida but are now classified in the genus Candidozyma.
Also known by the taxonomic synonym Epilobium, this hardy perennial in the willowherb family is native throughout the temperate north — which plant?
Chamaenerion angustifolium is a perennial herbaceous flowering plant in the willowherb family, Onagraceae.
Its Latin genus name literally means three-leaf, and this herbaceous legume, native to Europe, now grows worldwide in around 300 species — what plant is it?
Clover are plants of the genus Trifolium (from Latin tres 'three' and folium 'leaf').

This naturally occurring but largely inactive steroid hormone shields organs like the kidneys from active cortisol, and gets converted back into cortisol by an enzyme mainly in the liver — what hormone is it?
Cortisone is a naturally occurring, mostly inactive pregnene (21-carbon) steroid hormone.
Known mostly through DNA evidence rather than abundant fossils, this extinct group of archaic humans ranged across Asia between roughly 200,000 and 32,000 years ago — what are they called?
Denisovan (d-(nz)) are an extinct species or subspecies of archaic human that ranged across Asia during the Middle to Late Pleistocene, approximately 200,000-32,000 years ago.
Sometimes called word blindness, this learning disability makes reading, writing, or speaking difficult despite a normal desire to learn, and often overlaps with ADHD — name the condition?
Dyslexia is a learning disability that affects either reading, writing, or speaking.
This tightly coiled duct sits behind each testicle, serving as the crucial link to the vas deferens where sperm mature before their onward journey — what is it?
Epididymis (pl.: epididymides or) is an elongated tubular genital organ attached to the posterior side of each one of the two male reproductive glands, the testicles.

Discovered in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb in 1952 and named for a pioneer of nuclear physics, element 100 is the heaviest that neutron bombardment can produce. Which synthetic element is it?
Fermium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Fm and atomic number 100.

Discovered in Paris in 1875 and bearing the symbol Ga on the periodic table, this soft, silvery chemical element has such a low melting point — just below 30°C — that it turns liquid at warm room temperature. Name this element?
Gallium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ga and atomic number 31.
Comprising about 50 species native to tropical regions worldwide, this genus produces roughly 80% of the world's natural fiber and doubles as an oilseed crop — which genus?
Gossypium is a genus of flowering plants in the tribe Gossypieae of the mallow family, Malvaceae, from which cotton is harvested.
In their healthy state these vascular cushions in the anal canal actually help with stool control — it's only when they swell or inflame that they earn the nickname "piles." What are they?
Hemorrhoid (or haemorrhoids), also known as piles, are vascular structures in the anal canal.
This negatively charged ion, one oxygen bonded to one hydrogen, acts as a base and forms industrially vital salts like the sodium version used to make millions of tons of chemicals. What ion is it?
Hydroxide (occasionally hydroxyl ion) is a diatomic anion with chemical formula OH.

Acting as the eye's diaphragm in optical terms, this thin ring-shaped structure controls how much light reaches the retina by adjusting the pupil's size, and also determines a person's eye color — name this structure?

Iris (anatomy) (pl.: irides or irises) is a thin, ring-shaped structure in the eye in most mammals and birds that is responsible for controlling the diameter and size of the pupil, and thus the amount of light reaching the retina.
This Liverpool-born mathematician roamed from finite groups to knot theory, but is best loved for inventing a famous cellular automaton called the Game of Life — who was he?
John Horton Conway (26 December 1937 - 11 April 2020) was an English mathematician.
Named after a 19th-century Russian neuropsychiatrist, which memory disorder features confabulation and amnesia from vitamin B1 deficiency, often following an episode of Wernicke encephalopathy?
Korsakoff syndrome (KS) is a disorder of the central nervous system characterized by amnesia, deficits in explicit memory, and confabulation.

Named after the Italian word for lemon, this colorless liquid hydrocarbon is the main compound behind citrus peel fragrance, occurring mostly as a right-handed form extracted commercially by centrifugal separation or steam distillation - name the compound?

Limonene is a colorless liquid aliphatic hydrocarbon classified as a cyclic monoterpene, and is the major component in the fragrance and essential oil of citrus fruit peels, taking its name from Italian limone ("lemon").
This marsupial family native to Australia and New Guinea includes kangaroos, wallabies, quokkas, and tree-kangaroos among its 63 living species — what family is it?
Macropodidae is a family of marsupials that includes kangaroos, wallabies, tree-kangaroos, wallaroos, pademelons, the quokka, and several other groups.
First synthesized in 1982 near Darmstadt, this fleeting synthetic element of the periodic table's seventh period was named in 1997 after a pioneering Austrian-Swedish nuclear physicist. What is it?
Meitnerium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Mt and atomic number 109.

An Egyptian who studied architecture at Cairo University and worked as a civil engineer, this man was the oldest of the 19 hijackers and the ringleader who piloted American Airlines Flight 11 into the North Tower — who was he?
Mohamed Atta (September 1, 1968 - September 11, 2001) was an Egyptian engineer, architect, and the lead terrorist hijacker for al-Qaeda on American Airlines Flight 11.
This stocky Arctic whale carries a spiralled tusk up to three metres long — actually a protruding left canine tooth thought to serve as weapon, tool, and sensor — what is it?
Narwhal (Monodon monoceros) is a species of toothed whale native to the Arctic.
Belonging to the beech family and encompassing about 500 species across the Northern Hemisphere, this hardwood tree or shrub bears a distinctive nut held in a small cup — name the tree?
Oak is a hardwood tree or shrub in the genus Quercus of the beech family.
This Felidae subfamily, first described in 1917 as covering only the big cats, later expanded to include the clouded leopard genus as well — which subfamily?

Pantherinae is a subfamily of the Felidae; it was named and first described by Reginald Innes Pocock in 1917 as only including the Panthera species, but later also came to include the clouded leopards (genus Neofelis).
A self-described socialist active in Finland's Pirate Party, this entrepreneur co-founded a famous file-sharing search engine and later started the privacy service Njalla — who is he?
Peter Sunde (born 13 September 1978), alias brokep, is a Swedish-born Finnish-Norwegian entrepreneur and politician.

There are only five of these convex, regular three-dimensional shapes — including the cube, tetrahedron, and icosahedron — where every face is an identical regular polygon. What are these shapes called?
Platonic solid is a convex, regular polyhedron in three-dimensional Euclidean space.

Derived enzymatically from a fatty acid found in nearly every tissue of the body, this class of lipid compounds produces diverse hormone-like effects despite not being true hormones — what are they called?
Prostaglandin (PG) are a group of physiologically active lipid compounds that have diverse hormone-like effects in animals.
This transhumanist inventor who pioneered text-to-speech and OCR technology later won the $500,000 Lemelson-MIT Prize in 2001 for his work on artificial intelligence — who is he?
Ray Kurzweil (born February 12, 1948) is an American computer scientist, author, entrepreneur, futurist, and inventor.
Born in 1858, this German inventor devised a compression-ignition engine so significant that it and its fuel now both carry his surname — who was he?
Rudolf Diesel (18 March 1858 - 29 September 1913) was a German inventor and mechanical engineer.
This bodily fluid carries reproductive cells along with fructose and enzymes that help them survive their journey toward an egg — name the fluid?
Semen is a bodily fluid that contains spermatozoa from the male gonads of animals.

With the formula NaNO3 and historically mined in massive deposits in Chile, this white, deliquescent salt is a key industrial source used to make fertilizers, pyrotechnics, and explosives — which compound?
Sodium nitrate is the chemical compound with the formula NaNO3. The mineral form is also known as nitratine, nitratite or soda niter.
A Jamaican-British Marxist sociologist who co-founded New Left Review, this thinker became a founding figure of the Birmingham School of Cultural Studies — who was he?
Stuart Hall (cultural theorist) (3 February 1932 - 10 February 2014) was a Jamaican-British Marxist sociologist, cultural theorist, and political activist.
This American actress won an Oscar, three BAFTAs, two Tonys, and two Emmys, one of only 24 performers ever to complete acting's Triple Crown. Who is she?
Terry Gou (pinyin: Gu Timng; Peh-e-j: Koeh Ti-bng; born 18 October 1950) is a Taiwanese billionaire businessman and politician.
Caused by superantigens from staph or strep bacteria, this condition brings fever, a sunburn-like rash, and peeling skin, and has been tied to absorbent tampon use — which condition?
Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a condition caused by bacterial toxins.
This abnormal enlargement of the vein network draining the testicles is the most common correctable cause of male infertility, found in over a third of men with the condition. Name it?
Varicocele is an abnormal enlargement of the pampiniform venous plexus in the scrotum.
Neither an insect nor a parasite despite its common name, this terrestrial crustacean is one of the few of its kind to have colonized dry land, likely since the late Paleozoic — what is it?
Woodlouse are terrestrial isopods in the suborder Oniscidea.
Found naturally in coffee, bread and ripe fruit, this aldehyde is produced when your liver partly oxidizes ethanol — making it a chief culprit behind the hangover. What is it?

Born as a Spanish CASA design and now built by a major European aerospace conglomerate, this twin-engine turboprop transport plane first flew in November 1997 and entered Spanish Air Force service in 1999 — which aircraft?
Airbus C295: European tactical military transport aircraft.
A striking red-capped, white-warted mushroom of northern forests, this fungus may owe its name to an old use against flies — or to a medieval belief that flies caused madness. What is it?
Amanita muscaria: Species of mushroom. Amanita muscaria, commonly known as the fly agaric or fly amanita, is a basidiomycete fungus of the genus Amanita.

Multicellular eukaryotes that breathe oxygen and grow from a hollow ball of cells called a blastula, over 1.5 million species in this kingdom have been described by scientists. What are they collectively called?
Animal: Biological kingdom. Over 1.5 million living animal species have been described, of which around 1.05 million are insects, over 85,000 are molluscs, and around 65,000 are vertebrates.
Native to alpine lakes and polar coastal waters, this cold-water relative of salmon holds the title of the world's most northerly freshwater fish — what is it?
A cousin of the tomato and potato, this European nightshade is so toxic — via atropine and scopolamine — that even handling it can harm you; its other common name is "belladonna." What's the plant?
Atropa bella-donna: Deadly nightshade, a flowering plant.

Nicknamed the 'stone' or 'house' version of its family, this adaptable mustelid outcompetes its forest-specialist, pine-dwelling cousin in open habitats — and has even gone feral in North America. Which species is it?
Beech marten: Species of carnivore. It is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List on account of its wide distribution, its large population, and its presence in a number of protected areas.
Predicted by Einstein's general relativity, this astronomical body is so compact that not even light can escape past its event horizon. What is it?
Black hole: Compact astronomical body. A black hole is an astronomical body so compact that its gravity prevents anything, including light, from escaping.

This rare and potentially fatal illness comes from a toxin better known by its cosmetic nickname; it starts with blurry vision and slurred speech but usually spares both fever and consciousness — what is it?
He piloted the Lunar Module Eagle in 1969 to become the second person to walk on the Moon, and after Jim Lovell's death in 2025 became the oldest living astronaut — who is he?
Tetravalent and able to form four covalent bonds, this element known since antiquity ranks as the fourth most abundant in the universe by mass — which one is it?
Carbon: Chemical element with atomic number 6 (C)

Greek for "head-feet," fishers nickname these inkfish for their ink-squirting trick; their arms are muscular hydrostats modified from the primitive molluscan foot. Which marine class includes the octopus, squid, and nautilus?
Cephalopod: Class of mollusks. The study of cephalopods is a branch of malacology known as teuthology.
This form of cancer that begins in the tubes carrying digestive fluid from the liver can cause yellowing skin, dark urine, and pale stools — what is it?
Cholangiocarcinoma: Cancer of the bile ducts.
A tropane alkaloid drawn from the leaves of South American coca plants, it once served doctors as a local anesthetic with handy vasoconstricting properties — what is this stimulant?

Cocaine: Tropane alkaloid and stimulant drug. The leaves are processed into cocaine paste, a crude mixture of coca alkaloids, from which cocaine base is isolated and then converted to cocaine hydrochloride.
The first bomber capable of Mach 2 flight, this 1950s delta-winged bomber carried its nuclear payload in a combination bomb-and-fuel pod slung beneath the fuselage — which bomber?
Convair B-58 Hustler: Cold War-era American supersonic bomber.

Named after a mythological Greek youth transformed into a tree after killing his pet stag, this genus of evergreen conifers is found across warm temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere — which genus?
Cupressus: Several genera of evergreen conifers.
This field statistically studies human populations — their size and makeup — through the interplay of births, deaths, and migration — what is it?
Demography: Study of human populations and their structures.
Descended from the African wild ass and domesticated some 5,000 to 7,000 years ago, which working equine still numbers over 40 million worldwide?
Donkey: Domesticated animal primarily used for transportation.
Credited as the first to create a transuranium element — neptunium — this Berkeley physicist shared the 1951 Nobel in Chemistry with Glenn Seaborg. Who was he?
Also called Human Factors Engineering, this discipline applies psychology and physiology to reduce errors and boost safety in system design — what field?
Ergonomics: Designing systems to suit their users.
One of only two living species in its genus, this rodent was such a prized delicacy to the ancient Romans that its common name literally advertises the fact. What animal is it?
European edible dormouse: Species of rodent.
When fibroblasts overproduce collagen after repeated injury or chronic inflammation, this permanent connective-tissue scarring can impair an organ's normal function — what is it called?
Fibrosis: Excess connective tissue in healing.
Known for wood used in tool handles, electric guitars, and Morgan Motor Company's sports car frames, this tree genus produced nymphs called the Meliae in Greek myth — which genus?
Fraxinus: Genus of plants. The genus is widespread throughout much of Europe, Asia, and North America.
With a siphon that can stretch over three feet and a shell just 6 to 8 inches across, this giant Pacific burrowing clam can live up to 179 years — which creature?
Caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae and colloquially called 'the clap,' this sexually transmitted infection can pass from mother to child during birth — what is it?
Gonorrhea: Sexually transmitted infection. Gonorrhea or gonorrhoea, colloquially known as the clap, is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
This North Atlantic member of the true cod family is prized smoked as Finnan haddie or the Arbroath smokie — what fish is it?
Haddock: Species of fish. The haddock (Melanogrammus aeglefinus) is a saltwater ray-finned fish from the family Gadidae, the true cods.
This inflammation of the liver can cause jaundice and, if it becomes chronic, progress to cirrhosis — most commonly caused by five different viruses labeled A through E. What condition is it?
Hepatitis: Inflammation of the liver. Hepatitis is acute if it resolves within six months, and chronic if it lasts longer than six months.
The most widespread of all primates, this bipedal, nearly hairless species owes its advanced technology, culture, and language to a large, complex brain — what is it?
Human: Species of hominid in the genus Homo.

Extracted from a Central African plant sacred to Gabon's Bwiti tradition, this hallucinogenic alkaloid was once marketed in Europe as a stimulant before being studied for other therapeutic uses — what is it?
Ibogaine: Psychoactive substance found in plants in the family Apocynaceae.

A theoretical physicist who studied under Max Born earned a chemistry degree from Harvard before pivoting to nuclear physics — and later oversaw the first atomic weapons during WWII. Who is this pivotal figure in physics history?
J. Robert Oppenheimer: American theoretical physicist (1904–1967)
In a landmark 1913 Columbia University address, this American psychologist championed behaviorism and later became known for the unsettling 'Little Albert' experiment — who is he?
Nicknamed 'The Professor' on The Chase, this record-breaking contestant won 74 consecutive games on a legendary quiz show in 2004 before eventually becoming its host — who is he?
Ken Jennings: American game show host (born 1974)
Also called the Mediterranean black widow, this venomous spider is common throughout the Mediterranean region and central Asia — what species is it?

Latrodectus tredecimguttatus: Species of spider. Latrodectus tredecimguttatus, also known as the Mediterranean black widow or the European black widow, is a species in the genus Latrodectus of the widow spiders.
This Australian speech and language therapist and amateur stage actor helped King George VI manage his stammer — who is he?
Lionel Logue: Australian speech and language therapist (1880–1953)
Able to breathe air thanks to lobed fins and a well-developed internal skeleton, these freshwater vertebrates are considered the closest living relatives of land animals — what are they?
With horn-shaped fins on its head and one of the highest brain-to-body ratios of any fish, this filter-feeding giant may even recognize itself in a mirror — which creature?

Element 101, first made in 1955 by bombarding einsteinium with alpha particles, was the first that couldn't be produced by simply neutron-blasting a lighter element — and it honors the father of the periodic table. Which element is it?
Mendelevium: Chemical element with atomic number 101 (Md)
This Russian polymath discovered the atmosphere of Venus and formulated the law of conservation of mass, while also helping shape the modern Russian literary language as a poet — who is he?

Prized by gourmet cooks yet toxic if eaten raw or undercooked, this genus of honeycomb-capped edible fungi is difficult to cultivate, making wild harvests a multimillion-dollar industry — which fungal genus?
Morchella: Genus of fungi. Morchella, the true morels, is a genus of edible sac fungi closely related to anatomically simpler cup fungi in the order Pezizales (division Ascomycota).
Sold under the brand name Deca-Durabolin, this anabolic steroid is prescribed for conditions like anemia and osteoporosis despite masculinizing side effects — which compound?
Nandrolone: Androgenic Anabolic steroid. Nandrolone, also known as 19-nortestosterone, is an endogenous androgen.
Humphry Davy coined this colorless gas's cheerful nickname for the euphoria it brings, and it still earns a spot on the WHO's Essential Medicines list for dentistry and surgery. What is it?
Nitrous oxide: Colourless non-flammable greenhouse gas.

A subdiscipline of metaphysics, this philosophical study of being asks what reality's most general features are, sorting things into particulars like Socrates and universals like the color green — what is it?
Ontology: Philosophical study of being. For example, social ontology examines basic concepts used in the social sciences.
This cat-family genus contains the five biggest living cats — jaguar, leopard, lion, snow leopard, and tiger — plus extinct relatives like the cave lion and American lion. Which genus is it?
This genus of fungi is responsible for both a groundbreaking antibiotic and the mold that ripens certain blue cheeses — which genus?
Whether captured chemically on light-sensitive film or electronically by an image sensor, this art is fundamentally the practice of recording light — what is it?
Photography: Art and practice of creating images by recording light.
Whether natural silk or synthetic nylon, this class of polymer is defined by repeating units joined through amide bonds — what is it?
Polyamide: Macromolecule with repeating units linked by amide bonds.
Genetic studies trace this most widely cultivated apricot species to Central Asia, though its scientific name nods to a country in the Caucasus — what is it?
Prunus armeniaca: Species of apricot. The native range is somewhat uncertain due to its extensive prehistoric cultivation.
About the size of a house cat, this nocturnal herbivorous marsupial thrives on Rottnest Island near Perth and is the only member of its genus — what is it?
Quokka: Small marsupial from southwestern Australia.

Covering more than 200 conditions from arthritis to soft-tissue pain syndromes, this umbrella term for chronic joint and connective-tissue pain gives its name to a whole medical specialty — what is it called?
Rheumatism: Medical conditions affecting the joints or connective tissue.
Known as rue or 'herb-of-grace,' this Mediterranean plant is prized for its bluish leaves and doubles as an insect repellent — which species?
Ruta graveolens: Species of plant. Ruta graveolens, commonly known as rue, common rue, ruda, arruda or herb-of-grace, is a species of the genus Ruta grown as an ornamental plant and herb.
This group of autoimmune diseases causes thickened skin and poor blood flow to the fingers and toes, with one form known as CREST syndrome — what is it called?
Scleroderma: Group of autoimmune diseases resulting in abnormal growth of connective tissue.
Also called herpes zoster, this viral disease paints a painful blistering rash down just one side of the body, and can leave lingering nerve pain called postherpetic neuralgia — what is it?
Shingles: Viral disease caused by the varicella zoster virus.

Known as sun spiders, camel spiders, or wind scorpions, this arachnid order is neither true spider nor scorpion, and urban legends wildly exaggerate its size, speed, and danger to humans — what is it?
Solifugae: Order of arachnids. The order includes more than 1,000 described species in about 147 genera.
Fired by Apple's board in 1985, he founded NeXT and bought a animation studio before returning a decade later to revolutionize consumer tech. Who?
Steve Jobs: American businessman and inventor (1955–2011)
This Polish tax advisor turned politician placed third in the 2025 presidential election while chairing the libertarian New Hope party — who is he?
Sławomir Mentzen: Polish economist and politician (born 1986)
This large mass of gray matter sits between the cerebral cortex and the midbrain, relaying sensory and motor signals to the cortex while regulating sleep and alertness — what is this brain structure?
Thalamus: Structure within the brain. It has several functions, such as the relaying of sensory and motor signals to the cerebral cortex and the regulation of consciousness, sleep, and alertness.
This colorless solvent's sweet smell partly explains the aroma of gasoline and paint fumes, and its IUPAC name is simply methylbenzene — which aromatic hydrocarbon is it?
Toluene: Aromatic hydrocarbon. Toluene is a colorless, water-insoluble liquid with a sweet smell, and is partially responsible for the aroma of gasoline and paint fumes.
